5.3 Option Pricing

Put–call parity

Section titled “Put–call parity”

Start without any model, using only the absence of arbitrage (arbitrage). Take a stock that pays no dividends, and a European call and a European put on it, both with strike KKK and expiry TTT. Compare two portfolios:

  • Portfolio A: one call, plus a zero-coupon bond (zero-coupon bond) that pays KKK at expiry;
  • Portfolio B: one put, plus one share.

At expiry, if ST>KS_T > KST​>K, portfolio A exercises the call, uses the bond’s KKK to buy the share and ends with STS_TST​; in portfolio B the put expires worthless and it ends with STS_TST​. If ST≤KS_T \le KST​≤K, the call in portfolio A expires worthless and it ends with KKK; portfolio B exercises the put, sells the share at KKK and ends with KKK. Both portfolios pay max⁡(ST, K)\max(S_T,\ K)max(ST​, K) in every case, so their prices today must be equal:

C−P=S−Ke−rTC - P = S - K e^{-rT}C−P=S−Ke−rT

This is put–call parity. CCC and PPP are today’s prices of the call and the put, SSS is the stock price and Ke−rTK e^{-rT}Ke−rT is today’s price of the bond (continuous compounding, continuous compounding). It links the prices of four assets, the call, the put, the stock and the bond: given three of them, the fourth is determined, and a deviation allows arbitrage (Exercises Question 1). Like the forward price (5.1 Forwards and Futures), it makes no assumption about where the stock price will go.

Check C1
A stock pays no dividends. Its price is unchanged, but investors become more optimistic and now generally expect a higher return on it. By put–call parity, the call price minus the put price, for the same strike and expiry, becomes larger.
Look at both sides of the parity formula. Which of its quantities change when investors' expectations change?

The binomial model

Section titled “The binomial model”

Parity only gives the difference between a call and a put. To price a single option, we need an assumption about how the stock price moves. The simplest one is that after one period the price can take only two values. Suppose a stock is at 100 now and in one year will be either 120 or 90; the one-year risk-free rate is 4% (annual compounding). A one-year call with a strike of 100 pays 20 if the price goes up and 0 if it goes down.

A portfolio of stock and borrowing whose payoff is exactly the same as the option’s is called a replicating portfolio. Buy Δ\DeltaΔ shares and borrow BBB:

Δ=Cu−CdSu−Sd=20−0120−90=23\Delta = \frac{C_u - C_d}{S_u - S_d} = \frac{20 - 0}{120 - 90} = \frac{2}{3}Δ=Su​−Sd​Cu​−Cd​​=120−9020−0​=32​

If the price goes down, 23\frac{2}{3}32​ of a share is worth 60, just enough to repay the loan, so today we borrow B=601.04≈57.69B = \frac{60}{1.04} \approx 57.69B=1.0460​≈57.69. If the price goes up, 23\frac{2}{3}32​ of a share is worth 80; after repaying 60, 20 is left, the same as the option. Today the replicating portfolio costs

C=ΔS−B=66.67−57.69≈8.97C = \Delta S - B = 66.67 - 57.69 \approx 8.97C=ΔS−B=66.67−57.69≈8.97

Since the two pay exactly the same at expiry, the option’s price must be 8.97; otherwise one could buy the cheaper one, sell the dearer one and make an arbitrage profit. This method, which allows only an up move and a down move in each period and replicates step by step, is the binomial model. If the year is split into many short periods and Δ\DeltaΔ is adjusted in each one, the possible stock prices come close to a continuous distribution.

The same price can be written in another form. Let

p∗=(1+r)−du−d=1.04−0.91.2−0.9≈0.467p^* = \frac{(1 + r) - d}{u - d} = \frac{1.04 - 0.9}{1.2 - 0.9} \approx 0.467p∗=u−d(1+r)−d​=1.2−0.91.04−0.9​≈0.467

where u=1.2u = 1.2u=1.2 and d=0.9d = 0.9d=0.9 are the factors by which the stock price moves up or down. Then C=p∗×20+(1−p∗)×01.04≈8.97C = \frac{p^* \times 20 + (1 - p^*) \times 0}{1.04} \approx 8.97C=1.04p∗×20+(1−p∗)×0​≈8.97. p∗p^*p∗ is called the risk-neutral probability: if no investor cared about risk, the stock’s expected return would equal the risk-free rate, and p∗p^*p∗ is exactly the probability of an up move that makes the stock’s expected return 4%. Pricing by taking the expectation with p∗p^*p∗ and discounting at the risk-free rate is called risk-neutral pricing. What goes wrong if the probability of an up move that investors actually believe in is used instead? See Exercises Question 2.

Check C2
In the binomial example, the option's price was found without knowing how risk-averse investors are or the actual probability of an up move. The main reason is:

The Black–Scholes formula

Section titled “The Black–Scholes formula”

When the periods of the binomial tree become very short and the log return of the stock is normally distributed, that is, the stock price is lognormally distributed (lognormal distribution), the price of a European call has a formula, the Black–Scholes model:

C=S N(d1)−Ke−rTN(d2)C = S\,N(d_1) - K e^{-rT} N(d_2)C=SN(d1​)−Ke−rTN(d2​) d1=ln⁡(S/K)+(r+σ2/2) TσTd2=d1−σTd_1 = \frac{\ln(S / K) + (r + \sigma^2 / 2)\,T}{\sigma \sqrt{T}} \qquad d_2 = d_1 - \sigma \sqrt{T}d1​=σT​ln(S/K)+(r+σ2/2)T​d2​=d1​−σT​

N(⋅)N(\cdot)N(⋅) is the cumulative distribution function of the standard normal distribution (normal distribution), σ\sigmaσ is the stock’s annualized volatility (annualized volatility), and the put price follows from parity. The two terms can be read as follows: N(d2)N(d_2)N(d2​) is the probability, under the risk-neutral probabilities, that the option is exercised, and Ke−rTN(d2)K e^{-rT} N(d_2)Ke−rTN(d2​) is the present value of paying the strike if it is; S N(d1)S\,N(d_1)SN(d1​) is the present value of the stock received if it is exercised.

The formula has only five inputs: the stock price, the strike, the time to expiry, the risk-free rate and the volatility. Of these, only the volatility cannot be observed directly. Its assumptions include: volatility is constant over the life of the option; the stock price moves continuously, without jumps; and one can trade and sell short at any time without cost. None of these holds exactly; we will see the effects below.

The Greeks and hedging

Section titled “The Greeks and hedging”

The sensitivities of an option’s price to its inputs are written with Greek letters and called the Greeks:

  • delta: the derivative of the option price with respect to the stock price, ∂C∂S\frac{\partial C}{\partial S}∂S∂C​. A call’s delta is between 0 and 1, equal to N(d1)N(d_1)N(d1​) under Black–Scholes; a put’s delta is between −1 and 0. The Δ\DeltaΔ of the binomial tree is the delta.
  • gamma: the derivative of delta with respect to the stock price, that is, how curved the price curve is; it is largest near the money and close to expiry.
  • vega: the derivative of the option price with respect to volatility.
  • theta: the change in the option price as time passes, other things equal; a buyer’s theta is usually negative.

A market maker (market maker) who sells options usually does not want to bear the risk of the stock’s direction. After selling one call, he buys delta shares, so that small moves in the stock price have almost no effect on the position. This is called delta hedging, a form of hedging (hedging). It is also the idea behind the derivation of Black–Scholes: the option plus a continuously adjusted stock position forms a riskless portfolio, so the portfolio can earn only the risk-free rate.

Check C4
A market maker sells a batch of at-the-money calls and buys stock according to delta to hedge. The stock then jumps 10% in one day. As long as he does not trade again, his hedge still works: further moves in the stock price hardly affect his position.
After the jump, what happens to the delta of these calls? Has the number of shares he holds changed?

Implied volatility

Section titled “Implied volatility”

Of the five inputs to Black–Scholes, four can be observed directly. Turning it around, given an option’s market price, one can solve for the volatility that makes the formula give that price; this is the implied volatility. Option traders often quote only the implied volatility: it puts the prices of options with different strikes and expiries on one scale.

Implied volatility reflects how the market prices future volatility, not just past volatility. Cboe’s VIX index is computed from the prices of S&P 500 index options and measures how the market prices volatility over the next 30 days; it is usually between 12 and 25, and it went above 80 in November 2008 and in March 2020.

If the assumptions of Black–Scholes held exactly, options on the same underlying with the same expiry would have the same implied volatility whatever their strike. In practice they do not. For stock index options, the lower the strike, the higher the implied volatility tends to be; this is called the volatility skew. The pattern became clear after the stock market crash of October 1987.

Check C5
For stock index options, puts with strikes far below the current index level usually have higher implied volatility than at-the-money options. The most reasonable explanation is:
Low-strike puts are cheap anyway, even if every strike used the same volatility. What does implied volatility compare?
If everyone expected a fall, which price would reflect it first? Does implied volatility measure direction or the size of moves?
Parity rests only on no arbitrage and always holds for European options. By parity, how should the implied volatilities of a call and a put with the same strike compare?

Summary

Section titled “Summary”
  • Put–call parity, C−P=S−Ke−rTC - P = S - K e^{-rT}C−P=S−Ke−rT, depends only on the absence of arbitrage, not on any assumption about where the stock price will go.
  • The binomial model replicates an option with stock and borrowing; the option’s price equals the cost of the replicating portfolio. The same price is obtained by taking the expectation with risk-neutral probabilities and discounting at the risk-free rate.
  • The inputs of the Black–Scholes formula are the stock price, the strike, the time to expiry, the risk-free rate and the volatility; only the volatility has to be estimated.
  • Delta is the option price’s sensitivity to the stock price and also the number of shares needed to replicate or hedge it; gamma, vega and theta measure how delta changes and the sensitivity to volatility and to time.
  • Implied volatility is the volatility that makes the model price equal the market price; for stock index options it rises as the strike falls (the volatility skew).

Exercises

Section titled “Exercises”
Question 1
A stock that pays no dividends is at 50 dollars, and the continuously compounded risk-free rate is 5%. A 1-year European call with a strike of 50 costs 6 dollars, and the European put with the same terms costs 3 dollars.
(a) Are these prices consistent with put–call parity? If not, give a set of trades (which assets to buy or sell, and how many) that earns a riskless profit today, state the profit per share, and explain why there can be no loss one year later.
(b) A friend says: "At-the-money calls and puts should cost the same. The call is 3 dollars dearer than the put, so it is overvalued by 3 dollars." Evaluate this statement.
Question 2
A stock is at 100 dollars now and will be at 125 or 80 dollars in one year. The one-year risk-free rate is 5% (annual compounding). Consider a one-year European call with a strike of 100.
(a) Replicate the option with stock and borrowing: how many shares, and how much borrowing? What is the option's price?
(b) An analyst thinks the probability of an up move is 70%, so he computes the option's "true value" as 0.7×251.05\frac{0.7 \times 25}{1.05}1.050.7×25​ and says: "The market price is below the true value, so the option is undervalued and should be bought." Evaluate this statement: what would happen if the market price really equaled his value? If one insists on the 70% probability, what discount rate gives the price in (a)? Compared with the stock's expected return, is this discount rate reasonable?
Question 3
A firm's assets are worth 100 (million dollars) now, and its only debt is a zero-coupon bond with a face value of 90 due in one year. In one year, if the assets are worth more than 90, the firm repays the debt and the rest goes to shareholders; if less than 90, the shareholders, protected by limited liability, walk away and the creditors take all the assets. The continuously compounded risk-free rate is 4%, the annualized volatility of the asset value is 20%, and the Black–Scholes formula may be used.
(a) What form does the shareholders' payoff in one year take? Use this to value the equity and the debt today.
(b) Management can switch to a different business: the assets are still worth 100 today, but their volatility rises to 50%. The CFO says: "The firm's value does not change, so switching makes no difference to shareholders or creditors." Value the equity and the debt after the switch, evaluate this statement, and say how creditors can protect themselves.
Question 4
A company reports earnings after the close tomorrow. Its stock is at 100 dollars now, and a call with a strike of 100 and 0.1 years to expiry costs 7.74 dollars, an implied volatility of 60% (this stock's implied volatility is normally about 30%). The continuously compounded risk-free rate is 4%. An investor is sure the report will be good and buys this call.
(a) After the report, the stock rises to 105 dollars, the implied volatility falls back to 30%, and the option has 0.096 years left. By the Black–Scholes formula, what is the option worth now? With the same implied volatility and time left, how high must the stock go for him not to lose?
(b) He says: "I got the direction right and still lost on the option, so the market must be rigged." Evaluate this statement. Why was the implied volatility so high before the report? What must his view satisfy for buying the option to pay off?
